Well, three or four months went by, and winter was pretty well along. I’d attended school nearly all the time, and could spell and read and write a little, and recite the multiplication table as far as six times seven is thirty-five. I don’t suppose I’d get beyond that if I lived forever. Anyhow, I don’t put much faith in mathematics.

At first I couldn’t bear school, but after a while I learnt to stand it. When I got extra tired of it I played hookey, and the whipping I caught next morning done me good and brightened me up. So school got easier the longer I kept going. I was growing used to the widow’s notions, too, and they didn’t scrape on me so much. Staying in a house and sleeping in a bed generally cramped me considerable, but before cold weather came I would slip away and sleep in the woods now and then, and that rested me. I still preferred the old ways, though I was beginning to like the new ones a small amount. The widow said my progress was slow but certain, and she was well satisfied. She said she wasn’t ashamed of me.

One morning at breakfast I accidentally knocked the salt-cellar over. I grabbed for a pinch quick as I could, meaning to throw it over my left shoulder and turn away the bad luck. But Miss Watson got ahead of me and stopped me short. “Keep your hands back, Huckleberry,” she says; “you’re forever making a mess!” The widow spoke up kindly for me, but I knew well enough that wouldn’t drive the bad luck off. After breakfast I went out all troubled and shaky, wondering what form it would take and where it would strike me. You can ward off certain sorts of bad luck, but not this sort. So I didn’t attempt anything, and just wandered along downhearted, keeping watch.

I went into the front garden and climbed the stile through the tall board fence. Fresh snow lay an inch deep on the ground, and I noticed somebody’s footprints. They’d come from the quarry, stopped about the stile for a time, and then continued round the garden fence. It seemed queer that whoever it was hadn’t come inside after hanging about there. I couldn’t understand it. Somehow it struck me as mighty curious. I meant to follow them around, but first I bent down for a closer look at the tracks.

“I will do as you say. I can see in your face that you know I have no other choice. I know I can trust you.”

The old man kissed her, hurried her into his room, and locked the door. Then he rushed back to the Doctor, opened the window, raised the blind partway, and rested a hand on the Doctor’s arm. Together they looked into the courtyard.

They looked out on a crowd of men and women, neither numerous enough nor packed closely enough to fill the courtyard: forty or fifty people at most. Those occupying the house had opened the gate to them, and they had rushed in to use the grindstone. It had plainly been installed for them there, in a place both convenient and secluded.

But what horrifying workers, and what horrifying work!

The grindstone had two handles. Two men were turning them frantically, their long hair flying back whenever the stone’s revolutions brought their faces upward. Those faces were more cruel and terrible than the faces of the wildest savages in their most barbaric disguises. Fake eyebrows and moustaches were stuck to them. Their hideous features were drenched in blood and sweat, twisted with howling, their eyes staring and blazing with animal excitement and lack of sleep. While these brutes kept turning the stone, their tangled hair swinging over their eyes and back across their necks, women held wine to their mouths so they could drink. Between the dripping blood, the spilling wine, and the sparks streaming from the stone, the wicked air around them seemed made of fire and gore. Not one person in the group appeared free of bloodstains. Men naked to the waist, their limbs and bodies smeared with blood, shoved each other to take their turn at the sharpening stone. Men dressed in every sort of rag bore the same stains on their clothes. Others were grotesquely decorated with stolen women’s lace, silk, and ribbon, the blood soaking right through these ornaments. Hatchets, knives, bayonets, and swords brought for sharpening were all red with it. Some of the battered swords were fastened to their owners’ wrists with strips of linen and torn pieces of clothing. The bindings differed, but all were deeply soaked in that same color. As the frantic men snatched their weapons from the shower of sparks and rushed back into the streets, that red color blazed again in their maddened eyes—eyes that anyone who retained a trace of humanity would have given twenty years of life to freeze with a well-aimed shot.

“Yes, it is—and I could have got it myself if I’d been big enough. I saw him first. Who caught him?”

“An old man, a stranger. He sold his claim to him for forty dollars because he has to go upriver and can’t wait. Think of that! I’d have waited, even if it took seven years.”

“So would I,” I said. “But maybe his claim isn’t worth more than that, if he’s selling it so cheap. Maybe there’s something wrong with it.”

“There isn’t, though. It’s perfectly honest. I saw the notice myself. It describes him exactly, like a picture, and names the plantation he comes from, below New Orleans. No, sir, you can count on that being a good deal. Say, could you give me some chewing tobacco?”

I didn’t have any, so he went away. I returned to the raft and sat inside the shelter to think. But I couldn’t work anything out. I thought until my head hurt, without seeing any way out of our trouble. After that whole long journey, after everything we’d done for those villains, it had all come to nothing. Everything was wrecked because they were heartless enough to play that trick on Jim, making him a slave again for the rest of his life, among strangers too, for forty miserable dollars.

At one point I told myself that if Jim had to be a slave, it would be a thousand times better for him to be one back home with his family. Maybe I should write to Tom Sawyer and ask him to tell Miss Watson where Jim was. But I soon abandoned that idea for two reasons. She would be furious and disgusted at what she would call his wickedness and ingratitude in running away, and would sell him straight downriver again. Even if she didn’t, everyone naturally despised a Black man they considered ungrateful, and they would keep reminding Jim of it until he felt worthless and ashamed. And what about me? Word would spread that Huck Finn had helped a Black man escape slavery. If I ever met anyone from that town again, I’d be so ashamed I’d be ready to kneel and lick their boots. That’s how it goes: someone does something disgraceful, then doesn’t want to face the consequences. He thinks there’s no shame in it so long as he can hide it. That was exactly my position. The more I thought it over, the harder my conscience tormented me, and the more wicked, miserable, and worthless I felt.
